sections.name: securityHeaders
sections.title: Building the browser security header list
sections.what: Creates the content security policy and returns it with several other protection headers. Development mode adds one extra allowance that production does not get.
sections.why: Likely reason: every page gets the same protections from one place.
sections.watch_out: Editing the policy text can silently break scripts, styles or connections on every page.

summary: Builds the list of browser security headers that the site sends with every page, with extra allowances only in development.
purpose: Tells browsers what content they may load and how the site may be displayed, to block common attacks such as injected scripts and clickjacking.
why: The comment says these headers apply to every route through next.config.ts. Reason for the specific values is not stated in the code.
how: 1. Builds the content security policy as a list of rules joined into one text value. 2. Adds a development-only allowance for eval-style code when isDev is true. 3. Returns a list of header name and value pairs, including the policy, a no-sniff rule, a frame block, a referrer rule, a permissions block, a secure-connection rule and an opener rule.
inputs: isDev, a true or false flag saying whether the app is running in development.
outputs: A list of header name and value pairs for the server to send.
risks: The script rule allows inline scripts in every mode, which weakens protection against injected script. Any change here affects every page.
debug: If a page fails to load scripts, styles, images or connections, read the content security policy in the browser developer tools and compare it with the rules here. Confirm that next.config.ts calls this function.
